Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. $$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. Current consumer use and hypotheses: Definition item. Obligations: (i) the division by $\tau'$ is legitimate because $\tau'>0$ ([[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]); (ii) the equivalence $\dot P(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s))$ is the chain rule along the reparametrisation, $\rho$ being the inverse of the increasing function $\tau$; (iii) componentwise differentiation in one affine basis and change of basis commute because the transition map is constant and linear, so the definition is basis-free; (iv) no dynamics is imported: $F$ is a derived vector field attached to a given $P$, not a prescribed law. No choice principle is used. frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in the sense of
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain, and the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a) is the one proved in
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] for the encoded expressions; the statement of
this definition uses that regularity and adds no further analytic property.
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.. $u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class

$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$

Supplier quote: Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j<3}k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. Supplier quote: **Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. For beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1, where |beta| is the Euclidean norm, set gamma(beta) := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) >= 1, with equality exactly for beta=0 and strict inequality for beta!=0 (def-rational-power, lem-rational-power-laws). The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta is the linear map B(beta): V -> V defined by its action on coordinates: for beta not equal to 0, x'^0 = gamma (x^0 - beta . x),  x' = x + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . x) beta - gamma beta x^0, and for beta = 0, B(0) := identity, where x' denotes the coordinates of B(beta) applied to the vector with coordinates x, and beta . x is the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) the matrix of B(beta) is B^0_0 = gamma, B^0_i = B^i_0 = -gamma beta_i for i = 1,2,3, and B^i_j = delta^i_j + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) beta_i beta_j for i,j = 1,2,3 (with the last expression replaced by delta^i_j for beta = 0; the coefficient (gamma−1)/|beta|^2 tends to 1/2 as beta tends to0 through nonzero vectors, so the correction is (1/2) beta_i beta_j+o(|beta|^2) and the full spatial block tends to delta^i_j). In the 1+1 case beta = beta e_1 this reads x'^0 = gamma(x^0 - beta x^1), x'^1 = gamma(x^1 - beta x^0). The vector beta is called the boost parameter; it is dimensionless and mathematically independent of any unit convention. Let J: Omega -> V, k, and T be a C^k vector field, a C^k covector field and a C^k type-(r,s) tensor field on Omega in the sense of def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space, with components J^a, k_a and T^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s} in the chart x, and primed components in the chart x'. Then: (i) J'^a = Lambda^a_b J^b: a contravariant index gains the factor Lambda^a_b, i.e. components transform by multiplication with the transition matrix. (ii) k'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a k_b: a covariant index gains the factor (Lambda^{-1})^b_a. If theta(p) = k_a x^a(p) + theta_0 is an affine scalar function with constant covector k and constant theta_0, then theta(p) = k'_a x'^a(p) + theta'_0 with k' as above and theta'_0 := theta_0 - k'_a b^a, so the phase function is invariant when the constant term is transformed together with the covector. (iii) T'^{a_1...a_r}_{b_1...b_s} = Lambda^{a_1}_{c_1} ... Lambda^{a_r}_{c_r} (Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}_{b_1} ... (Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}_{b_s} T^{c_1...c_r}_{d_1...d_s}: every contravariant index gains a factor Lambda and every covariant index a factor Lambda^{-1}, and the law is consistent with the multilinear evaluation of T(p) after substituting the transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy eta'_{ab} = eta_{ab}. (iv) The coordinate partial derivatives satisfy partial'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a partial_b wherever the derivatives exist. Consequently the divergence of a vector field is invariant, partial'_a J'^a = partial_a J^a, and for a C^1 type-(2,0) field T one has partial'_a T'^{ab} = Lambda^b_c partial_a T^{ac}. (v) Alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies epsilon'_{abcd} = epsilon_{abcd}, since det Lambda = +1, whereas a general Lorentz matrix with det = -1 changes its sign. (vi) Let J be a C^1 vector field with components (J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3) in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as J_cov := (J^1,J^2,J^3) and denote by partial_i the spatial partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation partial_a J^a = 0 is equivalent to partial_0 J^0 + sum_i partial_i J^i = 0, and under the passive boost with parameter beta (Lambda = B(beta), Lambda^{-1} = B(-beta)) the components transform as J'^0 = gamma(J^0 - beta . J_cov), J'_cov = J_cov + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . J_cov) beta - gamma beta J^0. (vii) If U is a C^1 future timelike vector field and rho_0 a C^1 scalar field, then J:=rho_0 U is a C^1 vector field and its first component is J^0=rho_0 U^0. Future timelikeness gives U^0>0 in every inertial chart, so define the normalized chart direction u:=U/U^0 and the coordinate density rho:=J^0. Then u^0=1, u^i=U^i/U^0, rho=rho_0 U^0, and J=rho u pointwise. The coordinate density rho and scalar multiplier rho_0 are different objects: rho=rho_0 if and only if rho_0(U^0−1)=0; at points where rho_0!=0 equality holds exactly when U^0=1. The vector u is a normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity normalization. In an x^0=ct convention the associated spatial coordinate velocity, if interpreted as such, has components c u^i; physical current/density identification requires its own model premise. Interpretation boundary: the identification of a physical charge-current with a vector field, and of rho with a measured charge density, is a model premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert that any physical current transforms as a vector. Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula. Current consumer use and hypotheses: Proof strategy. (b) Write the worldline in proper-time parametrization, x = x(tau); then theta o x has derivative k(x'(tau)) = k(U(tau)) by (a) applied to the reparametrized curve, with the chain rule and the positivity of dtau/ds (lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization). (c) U is nonzero future timelike and k^sharp is nonzero future null, so eta(k^sharp,U) < 0 by lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative; by the defining property of k^sharp, k(U) = eta(k^sharp,U) < 0. (d) For an inertial observer, thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition(a),(d) gives eta(U,U) = -c^2 and the unit vector n = U/c; linearity gives k(U) = c k(n), and positivity is (c). Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

Exact supplied contract use: [{"fact": "F5", "source": "def-em-surface-distribution", "source_section": "Definition", "quote": "Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise

$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

[[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this
field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.. These are pointwise algebraic expansions; they assert no approximation of the trajectory over a time interval, which would require a separate stability argument. (d) [Scope] The charge is constant, $m>0$ is an externally supplied parameter and $F$ is a prescribed exterior field: the particle's own field, radiation reaction and any self-force are excluded, as are magnetic monopoles and zero or variable mass; the nonrelativistic coordinate law is not adopted as exact, and (c) is a controlled kinematic expansion, not a trajectory approximation.
